Content:
For instance, suppose that we want to plot the graph of [MATH: y = x^3-4x^2 +4x.] First, we need to find the roots, so we set [MATH: y=0] and solve:
[MATH: x^{3} − 4x^{2} + 4x|= 0; x(x^{2} − 4x + 4)|= 0; x(x − 2)^{2}|= 0]

Content:
By the zero-product rule, we get two distinct roots: [MATH: x=0] and [MATH: x=2.]

Content:
- The root [MATH: x=0] is a single root: it has multiplicity [MATH: {\color{blue}1}] because it comes from a factor [MATH: x^{\color{blue}1}] whose exponent is [MATH: {\color{blue}1}.]
- The root [MATH: x=2] is a double root: it has multiplicity [MATH: {\color{blue}2}] because it comes from a factor [MATH: (x-2)^{\color{blue}2}] whose exponent is [MATH: {\color{blue}2}.]

Content:
To graph the curve, we use the following principles:

Content:
- The curve passes through the [MATH: x]-axis at the single root (in this case, [MATH: x=0]).
- The curve touches the [MATH: x]-axis and turns around at the double root (in this case, [MATH: x=2]).

  • passes through the [MATH: x]-axis at the single root [MATH: x=2,] and

  • touches the [MATH: x]-axis and turns around at the double root [MATH: x=-1.]

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted [MATH: {\textsf{S}}]-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: (x-3)] is a factor of [MATH: f(x)=x^3+x^2-8x-12,] graph the curve [MATH: y=f(x).]
sections.readable_text: Given that [MATH: (x-3)] is a factor of [MATH: f(x)=x^3+x^2-8x-12,] graph the curve [MATH: y=f(x).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that [MATH: (x-3)] is a factor of [MATH: f(x),] so [MATH: (x-3)] divides [MATH: f(x).] To begin factoring [MATH: f(x),] we can divide it by [MATH: (x-3)] using synthetic division:

[MATH: x^{3}|x^{2}|x^{1}|x^{0}; 3|1|1|− 8|− 12; 3|12|12; 1|4|4|0]

Therefore,

[MATH: (f(x))/(x − 3)|= x^{2} + 4x + 4; f(x)|= (x − 3)(x^{2} + 4x + 4).]

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get [MATH: f(x) = (x-3)(x+2)^2.]

Now that we have the cubic in factored form, we can tell that it has a single root at [MATH: x=3] and a double root at [MATH: x=-2.]

We also find the [MATH: y]-intercept of the curve by substituting the value [MATH: x=0] into the equation:

[MATH: y|= (0 − 3)(0 + 2)^{2}; = (− 3)(2)^{2}; = − 12.]

So, the curve

  • intercepts the [MATH: y]-axis at [MATH: (0,-12),]

  • passes through the [MATH: x]-axis at the single root [MATH: x=3,] and

  • touches the [MATH: x]-axis and turns around at the double root [MATH: x=-2.]

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted [MATH: {\textsf{S}}]-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The graph of any cubic function [MATH: y = f(x)= ax^3 + bx^2 + cx +d,] where [MATH: a >0,] has a characteristic inverted [MATH: {\textsf{S}}]-shape, with [MATH: y]-values ranging from [MATH: -\infty] to [MATH: +\infty.] This means that every such function has at least one real root and at most three distinct roots.

Content:
For instance, suppose that we want to plot the graph of [MATH: y = x^3-4x^2 +4x.] First, we need to find the roots, so we set [MATH: y=0] and solve:
[MATH: x^{3} − 4x^{2} + 4x|= 0; x(x^{2} − 4x + 4)|= 0; x(x − 2)^{2}|= 0]

Content:
By the zero-product rule, we get two distinct roots: [MATH: x=0] and [MATH: x=2.]

Content:
- The root [MATH: x=0] is a single root: it has multiplicity [MATH: {\color{blue}1}] because it comes from a factor [MATH: x^{\color{blue}1}] whose exponent is [MATH: {\color{blue}1}.]
- The root [MATH: x=2] is a double root: it has multiplicity [MATH: {\color{blue}2}] because it comes from a factor [MATH: (x-2)^{\color{blue}2}] whose exponent is [MATH: {\color{blue}2}.]

Content:
To graph the curve, we use the following principles:

Content:
- The curve passes through the [MATH: x]-axis at the single root (in this case, [MATH: x=0]).
- The curve touches the [MATH: x]-axis and turns around at the double root (in this case, [MATH: x=2]).

Content:
Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted [MATH: {\textsf{S}}]-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/43f3cecbfe8e453d064d7ede08d95bd5]

---

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The equation is already in factored form, so by the zero-product rule, we deduce that it has a single root at [MATH: x=2] and a double root at [MATH: x=-1.]

We also find the [MATH: y]-intercept of the curve by substituting the value [MATH: x=0] into the equation:
[MATH: y|= (0 − 2)(0 + 1)^{2}; = (− 2)(1)^{2}; = − 2]

So, the curve

- intercepts the [MATH: y]-axis at the point [MATH: (0,-2),]
- passes through the [MATH: x]-axis at the single root [MATH: x=2,] and
- touches the [MATH: x]-axis and turns around at the double root [MATH: x=-1.]

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted [MATH: {\textsf{S}}]-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

[IMG: /graphics/a6e01d4213c63b8c6accbbfede4a08cc]
